notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0121i.stoa003.opp-l: Parenthetical source references (e.g. to the Lateran council of 649) are the edition's marginal citations of the passages the forger borrowed; they are kept as given. 'VI a propriis' read as 'vi' (by force). 'nec distingui a quoquam possunt': 'distingui' is probably corrupt for 'judicari' or similar; rendered 'judged'. The '(??)' is in the printed text. 'veluti palliati verbi per ventilabrum' is obscure, perhaps corrupt; rendered literally. 'Ipsam formam universorum titulorum' is uncertain in sense. The Job citation is given as Job 27 in the text but the passage is Job 29. 'die 17 kalendarum Augustarum' = 16 July.

Line 2.4: 'ad tempus veniat ad causam' rendered 'come in due time to the case'. Line 2.4a: 'episcoporum propositum ... prima fronte cedere' is obscure; rendered literally. Line 1a: 'Agath. Aur.' taken as the councils of Agde and Orléans. Line 5: 'ex Aniano' (the Breviary of Alaric, compiled by Anianus) left as a source marker. Line 1.4: the sentence ending 'dogmatica definitio' lacks a verb (presumably 'may shine'), as in the Latin. The numeral '3' before the heading in 2.head is a footnote mark and has been omitted.

VIII: 'inducite' read as 'induciae' (delays granted to the accused); 'exposcent' read as 'exposceret'. The clause 'ut in loco unde est ille qui accusatur' lacks a verb; '[the case is heard]' is supplied. XI: 'boc' read as 'hoc'; 'quampiam' is odd (perhaps for 'quaepiam'). XIII: 'suis calamitatibus altis' makes little sense; read as 'suis calumniis aliis' ('to disparage others with their slanders'). XIV: the quotation is 1 Corinthians 2:15, though the edition cites II Cor. II. XIX: 'Asclepius' (with footnote mark) taken as Asclepas of Gaza, and 'Lucianus Adrianopolites' as Lucius of Adrianople, the bishops known from the sources; the text's forms are 'Asclepius' and 'Lucianus'.

In 2.21, 'non lautum ipsi sunt decidentes' is read as 'non tantum' (not only); in 3.4, 'ad lautam ... iniquitatem' is read as 'tantam' (such great). The consuls 'Agarius and Julian' and 'Philemon and Atticus' are fictitious datings of the forgery and not securely identifiable. 'Lucianus Adrianopolites' etc. not relevant here. In 3.4 'palo excutere palum' is a proverb (cf. 'nail drives out nail'); 'nigella' (fennel-flower) with the reference Daniel III is obscure and the sense uncertain. The passage on the 'dwelling' (inhabitaculum) is syntactically confused in the source (translated from the Lateran acts) and is rendered closely. The quotation 'Scripsi enim vobis... per multas lacrymas' is cited as I Cor. II but is II Corinthians 2:4. 'Quaerens quaere' (Isa. 21:12 LXX) rendered 'If you seek, seek'.

nodes.text: LETTERS AND DECREES.
LETTER
OF ST ATHANASIUS AND THE BISHOPS OF EGYPT TO POPE FELIX II.
On the attacks of the Arians.

To the most blessed and honourable lord, the holy father Felix, pope of the holy apostolic see of the city of Rome, Athanasius and all the bishops of the Egyptians, the Thebaids and the Libyans, gathered by the grace of God in the holy synod of Alexandria.

We suggest to your holy (Maurus, bishop of Cesena, to St Martin; session 1 of the Lateran council, in the year 649) apostolate that you see fit, as is your custom, to take care for us, in accordance with your most prudent wisdom, which is plainer than light to all: for your beatitude, moved in its apostolic heart (Deusdedit, bishop of Cagliari, to St Martin) over our tribulation, has urged us all to come together into one for the defence of the catholic and apostolic Church, and to deal canonically and unanimously with our oppression, since it is clear that you, together with the blessed apostle Paul, say the same things with fellow-feeling: Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn (II Cor. 11:29)? taking pains that none of the rational sheep entrusted to you be seized by beasts. Therefore, most blessed father, because our predecessors and we ourselves have always drawn help from your holy apostolic see, and have recognised that you take care of us, we seek out the aforesaid apostolic and supreme see, according to the decrees of the canons, so that we may take help from the place from which our predecessors took ordinations, doctrines and relief. To it also we run back as to a mother, that we may be nourished at her breasts, since a mother cannot forget her infant. So you too, do not forget us who are entrusted to you, since our enemies have entangled us in no light afflictions, and daily strive to do so, and threaten to seize us or have us bound in irons (Stephen of Dor to the same pope, session 2 of the same synod), unless we consent to their errors: which we would by no means presume to do without consulting you. For the canons command that we ought to decide nothing concerning major cases without the Roman pontiff. And so, returning to our purpose, and hastening towards the prize, we implore the help of your apostolic see: because, as we believe, God has not despised the prayers offered to him with tears by his servants, but for this reason he set you and your predecessors, that is, the apostolic prelates, in the citadel of the summit, and commanded them to have care of all the churches, so that you may come to our aid, and, protecting us, you to whom all judgement of bishops is committed, may not neglect to free us from our enemies. For we know that in the great synod of Nicaea of three hundred and eighteen bishops it was confirmed by all with one accord that councils ought not to be held without the judgement of the Roman pontiff (Socrates, book II, chapters 8 and 17; Sozomen, book III, chapter 9), nor bishops condemned, although these and very many other necessary synodal chapters have been burned and taken from us by the heretics who attack us daily and strive to destroy us, so that they may seize us more easily. Wherefore, having found this occasion, without distinction, setting aside all canonical and apostolic authority, they unlawfully expel us by force from our own sees without consulting you: and they invade the sheep entrusted to us by Christ the Lord through apostolic grace, deprive [them] of their ranks, and, what is worst and hostile to all Christian laws, strive to kill [them]. You therefore (as has always been the custom of your holy see) come to the aid of those in danger, strengthen the oppressed, stretch out a hand to the afflicted, forbid such things, and impose laws, so that the apostolic teaching, which is in God, may swiftly bring our judgement to victory, and (with Peter, the prince of the apostles, lending his support) free us from the dangers that threaten. For we know that in the aforesaid synod of Nicaea (And it is found in the decretal letter of Julius against the Easterners on behalf of Athanasius, chapter 7) it was decreed generally that no one should presume indiscriminately and at random either to tear at bishops presumptuously, or to accuse them, and that those who are not of right faith, or of good life, or of distinguished conduct, should not presume to defame them: but first, if anyone has a case against bishops or the authorities of the Church, let him approach them gently with charity, so that the wound in question may be rightly healed by them: or if he does otherwise, let the accuser himself be excommunicated. But if he can obtain nothing rightly from them, then let him first approach the chief primates, and they, at a suitable time, will be obliged to summon them canonically (Ibid., chapter 17). If they have either been stripped of their property, or ejected from their own sees, or are in exile, or oppressed or unjustly treated, let them first be rescued and canonically restored (Ibid., chapter 8), and let everything taken from them be returned to them in full by the laws (Hadrian's collection, 35): since before these things are done (as was laid down in the aforesaid council), they can neither be canonically summoned nor judged by anyone, since not even the laws of the world permit these things to be done, how much less the laws of the Church! Likewise it was defined in agreement by the aforesaid fathers that if any of the bishops should hold his metropolitans, or his fellow-provincials, or his judges suspect, he should appeal to your holy Roman see, to which the power of binding and loosing (Matthew 16) was granted by the Lord himself by special privilege above others. For it (Sergius, bishop of Cyprus, to Theodore, session 2 of the Lateran council) received a foundation fixed by God and immovable, since the Lord Jesus Christ established your apostolic see as the most shining pattern of all titles. For it is the sacred summit on which all the churches turn, are sustained and are raised up. (??) And as Christians in Christ, and Peter in the rock, that is Christ, so the churches of Peter are renewed. For you are (as the divine word truly testifies) Peter, and upon your foundation the columns of the Church, that is, the bishops, who ought to sustain the Church and carry it on their own shoulders, have been confirmed for you, and he entrusted to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and proclaimed [that you] bind and loose with power things that are on earth and in heaven (Matthew 16). You are the deposer of profane heresies, of assailants and of all attackers, as prince and teacher, and the head of all orthodox doctrine and spotless faith. Do not therefore despise, father, the piety and good intention of your fathers. And as they freed our fathers and predecessors from many oppressions and straits, so may you see fit to free us. For your holy and apostolic see has always had licence to restore with power, by its own authority, those unjustly condemned or excommunicated, and to return all their property to them, and to punish by apostolic privilege those who condemned or excommunicated them, as we know was done both in our times and in earlier ones. Moreover, the primates themselves, who ought to take up the cases of bishops and of the highest ecclesiastical matters, were enumerated in the aforesaid synod of Nicaea, so that no contention should arise from this in future. O most holy father of fathers (The same bishop Sergius, just cited), cut off the blasphemies and boasting of empty talkers, and the attacks of those who lie in wait, who oppress us and our brothers and wish to destroy us, who flee to you as to the head, so that, supported by your help, we may be freed, and may snatch the sheep of Christ entrusted to you and to us from the mouth of the wolves, with the Lord's aid, before they are swallowed. For it is not right (Pope St Martin, in the same place) to despise the prayers offered by suppliants of the apostolic see, in writing or without writing, but (as is fitting, and as is the privilege of your see) let both we and they be canonically summoned, and let us contend canonically before you with all probity concerning the charges against us, as our predecessors did before your predecessors, and as the canonical institutions in the aforesaid holy synod teach, and as of a cloaked word, through the winnowing-fan of canonical examination; standing in a common hearing, let us obtain full purgation, concerning the ripe and nourishing doctrines of the catholic Church which strengthen the heart of man, through participation in the institutions of the fathers. For it was laid down by ancient rules (The African fathers in their letter to Pope Theodore, session 2 of the Lateran council held in 649) that whatever was done concerning complaints or accusations against bishops, even in provinces set far off or remote, should not be dealt with or accepted before it had been brought to the notice of your kindly see, so that by its authority the pronouncement, whatever it had been, might be weakened or confirmed: and that they should take their norm from the place from which the churches took the beginning of their preaching, and that the columns of the Church should not be overthrown at random by those lying in wait. For it is certain that the decrees of the fathers decreed to this same holy see of yours, in honour of most blessed Peter, a special reverence of God for investigating and determining matters, which ought to be examined carefully and justly by that apostolic summit of prelates, whose concern always was and is both to condemn evil things and to approve things worthy of praise. Wherefore, paying most humble obedience to your apostolic eminence, as the Lord himself commanded and the decrees of the holy fathers have laid down, we suggest with tears what we cannot keep silent without groaning of heart. For we are persecuted to such a degree by the persecutors of the holy Church of God and by our enemies that we are wearier of living than of dying. Hence above all we confess that our heart is so wounded (Victor of Carthage in his letter to Pope Theodore) that we long for that prophetic lament, saying: Who will give water to our head, or a fountain of tears to our eyes, that sitting we may weep day and night (Jeremiah 9)? For behold, the Church of God is disturbed in no light way, and its columns are greatly attacked, and wicked men strive to remove them. The voices of Christians and the groans of bishops resound far and wide; novelties rise up, slanders grow, persecution rages, the ruin of peoples comes about. For it is yours to stretch out a hand to us, since we are entrusted to you. It is yours to defend and free us; and it is ours to seek help from you and to obey your commands. Because of excessive grief and groaning, therefore, we are unable to recall all the things that press upon us and attack us, and to make them known to you. Therefore we beseech your kindly apostolate that concerning these things you restore the law that was promulgated in the aforementioned synod of Nicaea, although it has been suppressed by the corruption of the aforesaid plotters and of other evil men (so that they may the more easily ensnare bishops and ministers of God): and that by the authority of your holy see you instruct us and all our brothers in what you know will be necessary, so that, supported by your authority, we may escape unharmed, with the Lord's help, the plots of evil men: for it is not for the sheep to foresee the plots of wolves (Third Council of Rome under Symmachus), but for the shepherds. For we know (as the prelates of your see have always done, first the apostles, then their successors) that you ought to take care of the universal Church, and especially of the bishops, who are called the eyes of the Lord because of contemplation and watching, and to think constantly about our revelation and law, as it is written: Blessed is the man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night (Psalm 1): which meditation (Victor of Carthage, letter cited) is not perceived by reading through the shapes of letters only, but, with the grace of Christ overflowing in you, is recognised as immovably implanted in your conscience, the most holy law of Christ, God and Lord, in no way departing from your heart, as the prophet says in the psalm: The mouth of the just will meditate wisdom, and his tongue will speak judgement: the law of his God is in his heart (Psalm 36): written in your inmost parts not with ink but with the spirit of the living God; not on tablets of stone but on fleshly tablets of the heart (II Cor. 3), as the letter of the most blessed apostle Paul sent to the Corinthians teaches us. Having set these things forth, we make known to your paternity, pleasing to God, that on the sixteenth of July, in the fourth indiction, our humility, by divine grace, its gift (as it commanded) going before, through your holy and God-worthy prayers, received in the holy Roman Church the consecration and stole of pontifical honour: in which height of dignity, that we may be ruled by almighty God most high and freed from all evils, so that we may have not only the priestly name but, with the protecting help of Christ our Lord God, the merit also, commending ourselves to your holy and God-acceptable prayers, we ask that, fortified by your supplications poured out to God for us and instructed by good teachings, we may be made worthy, together with all the Christian people entrusted to us, to be protected unharmed by the divine veil. For the greeting of your holy and honourable paternity in our stead, therefore, we have sent Benedict, your humble brother, our bishop, and Alexander the priest, and also Crispinus the deacon, your servants, whom we ask your beatitude to send back to us quickly, so that, strengthened by your exhortations and instructed by your rules, our enemies being suppressed, we may, prudently consoled, be able to return to our own churches before winter, God willing. For it is yours, most holy father, with canonical strictness (See the end of the same letter of Victor), carefully to oppose those who go against the ecclesiastical rule and those who lie in wait for the brothers, and not to allow to be newly said what the authority of the venerable fathers in no way approved. For we, humble of heart, minding with the Lord's help the things that are right, are bound to you by one bond of charity, strongly defending in all things the true faith and catholic religion. Catholics must therefore strive the more zealously to resist the wicked uprightly, lest, overcome and torpid with sloth, we be held liable for the fault of silence, and be judged as if granting favour, while we neglect to repel things hostile to the catholic faith. Hence it has been said: For to neglect to throw down the perverse when you can is nothing other than to cherish them. Nor is he free from the suspicion of secret partnership who ceases to oppose a manifest crime. It is clear, most holy teacher, that the venomous cunning of serpents, without simplicity, is manifest as the deceitful falsehood of our enemies. Help the oppressed, we beg, free us from the hand of those who persecute us, so that you may sing with blessed Job: The blessing of him who was about to perish came upon me, and I comforted the heart of the widow. I put on justice, and clothed myself with my judgement as with a garment and a diadem. I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame. I was a father of the poor, and the cause I did not know I investigated most diligently. I broke the millstones of the wicked, and took the prey from their teeth (Job 29), and the rest. For we whom your very great care awaits (Innocent, letter 18 to Alexander of Antioch), that is, all the bishops, ought above all to merit your judgement, and not to be devoured by others. Rightly then does the Lord's cause regard us priests, if by silence we favour error (Celestine, letter 1 to the Gauls). Let such people indeed be rebuked, and let them not be free to make judgement at will. Let novelty cease to assail antiquity; let unrest cease to disturb the quiet of the churches. For so that all metropolitans or other bishops may not be able to exercise their hatreds or vengeance on the other bishops, the primates were therefore expressly named in the synod of Nicaea, who should hear and judge the other bishops, so that no fraud may burst in upon the judgement of bishops. You, therefore, who by the grace of God have been placed on the highest watchtower, ought to watch out for and suppress those who stir up seditions and scandals against the brothers (Stephen of Dor to the Lateran synod, year 619). And therefore we beseech you not in the least to despise the afflictions of our humility and of all the orthodox priests and peoples of the East, and the entreaties offered with tears, but, as lights to the whole world, holding fast the word of life, extinguish the darkness that has been brought in by the most wicked of those who lie in wait, which has sprung up insolently even in our own times, so that, once this gloom has been utterly extinguished, the morning star may shine again for us through you, most holy father, and the dogmatic definition, gladdening all everywhere, which the glorious fathers of the holy Church are known to have proclaimed through their own most pious dogmas as a firm inheritance of eternal life.
May the Lord keep you safe and well-pleasing to God (Sergius of Cyprus, letter to Pope Theodore, cited above), most holy father of fathers, praying for us, for ever. Amen.
FIRST LETTER OF POPE FELIX II.
REPLY TO THE BISHOPS GATHERED IN THE SYNOD OF ALEXANDRIA.

I. That no one should accuse a bishop before secular arbiters.—II. If anyone has a case against a bishop.—III. On the same.—IV. On bishops despoiled of their property or driven from their see.—V. That the infamous and sacrilegious are not to be admitted to testify.—VI. If a bishop summoned to a council cannot go.—VII. On cases which are not contained in the laws, or are known to be prohibited.—VIII. On accusations of bishops, and the restoration of their property that has been taken away.—IX. Who may not accuse or testify.—X. On the same matter.—XI. On the persons of accusers.—XII. On primates and metropolitans.—XIII. On accusations of bishops, and the unfitness of accusers.—XIV. Who ought not to be admitted to make an accusation.—XV. On the same matter.—XVI. That in ecclesiastical business it is permitted, once a case has been pleaded and concluded, to withdraw, which is not permitted in secular business.—XVII. On accusations of bishops.—XVIII. On not deciding the cases of bishops without the authority of the Roman pontiff.—XIX. If a bishop feels himself oppressed by the bishops of his province or by the metropolitan.—XX. On the judgements of bishops, and on the time granted for preparing and appearing.—XXI. On judges and accusers, what kind they ought to be.

To the most reverend and most beloved brothers, Athanasius and all the bishops of the Egyptians, the Thebaids and the Libyans, gathered in the holy synod of Alexandria, Felix, bishop of the gracious city of Rome and of the universal Church, and the holy synod which has assembled in the city of Rome: greeting in the Lord.

Your sacred synodal letter, written through the grace of the Holy Spirit and with a zeal pleasing to God, we gladly received for the sake of your holiness, to be honoured by God, and we immediately ordered it to be read out point by point in the synod, and instructed all to take in its words attentively. While we hoped and longed to rejoice over them, our lyre was turned to mourning, our song to weeping, and all the joy of the whole synod was changed into grief (Job 30): for it was not fitting that those who daily make the body of Christ with their own mouth (St Jerome, in the letter to Nepotian) should suffer so great a persecution, since the Lord our God, providing for the salvation of the human race, commanded that persecutions should not take place, nor disturbances be brought on, nor those labouring in the Lord's field be envied, nor the stewards of the great king be harassed or expelled. Be still, says the great holy synod of Nicaea (6, question 1), and do not persecute those who minister perfectly to God, and with sincere will keep the commands of God on high, and are subject to our laws; for it is neither fitting, nor does order permit, that the wicked and carnal should persecute the spiritual. For everyone who resists someone, now by twisting, now by concealing the truth, lies against the one with whom he is in dispute. And whoever is hostile to someone does everything as an enemy, and moreover strives to speak [against him]. We therefore admonish you, brothers, that you ought to be on the watchtowers, so that as far as you can, and as the Lord gives help, you may resist such people by our apostolic authority and yours, and let none of you withdraw himself from a brother's aid, but let him give support according to his strength. For although you are few, if you are of one mind, you will by no means be overcome, with justice supporting you and the Lord also bringing aid, because a threefold cord is hard to break (Ecclesiastes 4). For if human law comes to the aid of secular offices (St Gregory, letter 120, book 7), how much more ought divine and catholic law to support ecclesiastical [offices] and the priests of the Lord, and above all the bishops, who are called the pupils of the Lord's eyes! For the divine word says of bishops: Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye (Zechariah 2). And if secular men are examined in many ways by human law, and its inquiries and delays of many months are granted, lest they be unjustly condemned: how much more ought much longer periods be granted to bishops, who are nearer to God, and set over these, and placed in the heavenly warfare, which must be weighed more carefully, so that they are not burdened, oppressed or suddenly condemned by certain people! Let us begin, then (Innocent, letter 2), with the help of God and of the holy apostle Peter, through whom the apostolate and the episcopate in Christ took their beginning, since many cases have often arisen which in some instances were not cases but crimes, because, as we have learned, they were laid upon the brothers more out of wickedness than out of charity; and so that for the future there may be care that such things do not happen, let us set down certain chapters established by the holy fathers both in the synod of Nicaea and in this see, supported by which our brothers and fellow bishops may, with the Lord's help, be able to escape the snares of their enemies; and, as the Lord grants the ability, let us in fewer words make a summary of such great evils (the same pope, letter 7), and briefly go over what we found in the volume of your letter, and set down some other things necessary for the present time, as you request.
I. For it has been decreed by synodal institutions (Carthage III, c. 9; Milevis 19; Agde; Orléans, etc.) that no one should accuse a bishop before secular arbiters, but before the highest primates.

II. If anyone has a case against a bishop, let him not approach any bishops to accuse him before he has made his complaint known to him privately, and has received from him either a just amendment or a reasonable excuse, as the Truth itself instructs us: If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone (Matthew 18). If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. If he does not listen to you, take two or three with you; and if he does not listen to these, tell the Church (Luke 17), that is, accuse him publicly, and not before, and the rest.

III. If after this anyone chooses to accuse a bishop, let him make his case known to the highest primates of the bishops, and not to secular persons; and let them call them back to peace rather than to judgement (Carthage IV, c. 26), so that charity may be kept in all things and by all. If the primates (5, question 2) are quite unable to reconcile the accusers of bishops with them privately, then at a lawful time let them canonically summon them to a canonically convened synod, not within a short time, and not before they have informed them in writing what is charged against them, so that they may come prepared to answer. For if they have been ejected by force (Roman Council V, under Symmachus) or by fear, or despoiled of their property, they can neither be canonically summoned to a synod nor ought they to answer their rivals before they are canonically restored and all their property is lawfully returned to them.

IV. If any of the bishops has been despoiled of his property, or expelled from his church by force or fear, which is hostile to the whole Christian name, it is proper and fitting that the bishops' resolve should always give way at the first instance, so that everything taken from him is lawfully returned to his control, and the prelate is first restored; and afterwards, not at once but over a long and ample time, having arranged his affairs with full authority and prepared for his needs, let him come in due time to the case, and, if it seems just, answer his accusers.

V. Let no infamous or sacrilegious person be permitted to give testimony in any matter whatever against a religious Christian, however humble and servile a person he may be, nor to assail a Christian on any matter, by action or by written charge.

VI. If any bishop has been lawfully accused and canonically summoned to a council in the aforesaid order, he must go without any hesitation; and if he cannot go (Hadrian, c. 5), let him send a legate to the synod in his place.
VII. No cases shall be heard by ecclesiastical judges (the same, c. 11) that are not contained in the laws, or that are known to be prohibited.

VIII. If anyone will not rest content otherwise than by accusing a bishop, he must proceed in the manner set out above, because otherwise the accusation cannot stand as valid. Then, first, let the accuser canonically bring the case of the accused before the primates (Carthage III, 7). Nor let the accused be barred from communion, unless, having been canonically summoned to the judgement of chosen [judges], he has put off coming within three or six or more months to render account for his affairs. But if he can prove that he was not unwilling but unable to come, it will do him no harm. But he who has been driven from his see by force or fear, or despoiled of his property, shall not be summoned to a synod before everything has been restored to him according to the laws. And let him remain in his own see, peacefully arranging everything with full authority, for as long as he was seen to be deprived of his property while expelled or despoiled (Roman [synod] V, under Symmachus) (3, q. 2; and in the decretum of Ivo, book XLIII, q. 3). And when he comes to judgement, if he wishes and it is necessary, let the delays established by the fathers be granted to him at his request without hindrance, and let judges chosen by himself be assigned to him, so that [the case is heard] in the place where the accused comes from; or, if he fears the violence of some reckless crowd elsewhere, let him choose a place suitable to himself, where without fear he may have his witnesses, if need requires (African Council, c. 30), and may bring his canonical sentence to an end without hindrance, because many things tend to happen through underhand dealing.

IX. That the right of testifying or accusing be denied to those who have disregarded the dignity of the Christian religion and name, and the norm of their own law or their own profession, or [have committed] what is prohibited by rule (Anianus on c. 1, tit. 7, book XVI of the Theodosian Code).

X. Disparagement prevails greatly when the disparager is believed (Tripartite [History] III, 8; from Socrates I, 31). Therefore it is not fitting that a primate be undermined by various detractions and accusations, but rather that he be strengthened by the rules of the fathers (Damasus, letter to the Illyrians, in Theodoret II, 22). Nor let him presume to accept accusations readily or indiscriminately, since the Lord says: You shall not accept the voice of a lie (Exodus XXIV); but he must first test the suspicion and the cause, or with what intent [the accuser] does this, and afterwards accept [it]: because the aim of kinship, enmity, fear, love, hatred and greed tends to obstruct the profession of truth (Anianus on book V of the Sentences of Paul, tit. 15, sent. 2), and to inflict harm on the brethren.

XI. The persons of accusers (Hadrian, 4 and 15) ought to be such that their faith, conduct and life are approved and beyond reproach, and that they are free of all suspicion: because this too, in your presence, as you well know, was defined by all at the synod of Nicaea on account of the harassment of wicked men, although these and some other [decrees] have been destroyed by the plots of depraved men.

XII. Let those be primates, and no others, who were established at the synod of Nicaea. But the rest, who hold metropolitan sees (Hadrian, coll. 23), are called archbishops and not primates, saving in all things the dignity of the apostolic see, which was granted to it by the Lord himself, and afterwards confirmed by the holy fathers.

XIII. Always first (the same, c. 15), in every accusation of bishops, let the life, person and conduct of the accusers be examined in detail; and afterwards let the charges brought be faithfully dealt with: since nothing ought to be done otherwise than that the good faith of the accusers is first inquired into, and their persons, life and acts are examined: because the life of the innocent ought not to be torn apart by the malice of depraved or scheming men. Indeed, very often the good are persecuted by the wicked, who do not cease to disparage others with their slanders. Therefore the greatest care must be taken that these things do not happen.

XIV. Let no slave (Carthage VII, c. 2), no freedman, no faithless person, no one entangled in crimes, no slanderer, no one who pursues enmities, no one who frequently goes to law (Hadrian 11 and 50, from Carthage IV, 58, and VII, 2) and is ready to accuse or detract, no infamous person, nor any of those whom the public laws do not admit to accuse public crimes, be permitted to accuse bishops; for I cannot find by what reasoning the priestly order ought to accept accusers and accusations which the laws of the world do not accept, since these things were also forbidden at the synod of Nicaea, and those ought rather to be judged by these, not these by those; and the apostle says: The spiritual man judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one (II Cor. II).

XV. Heretics, by whom we are greatly oppressed, and the excommunicated, murderers, sorcerers, thieves, the sacrilegious, robbers, poisoners, adulterers, and those who have committed abduction, or have given false testimony, or who have resorted to fortune-tellers and magicians (Hadrian, coll. 63), shall in no way be admitted to accusation or to testimony.

XVI. Nor is one to act in ecclesiastical matters as in secular ones (St Leo, letter 54). For in secular matters, after someone has come when summoned by the laws and has begun to contend in court, he may not withdraw before the case is concluded: but in ecclesiastical matters, once the case has been stated, one may withdraw, if it is necessary, or if he sees that he is being unduly burdened.

XVII. Whenever a bishop (Hadrian 27) is accused of specific crimes, if the accusers are such as ought justly and canonically to be accepted, let him be heard canonically by all the bishops who are in the provinces, in a lawful synod assembled at its proper time. But if the accusers are not lawful, let the bishop not be harassed: because priests ought to be free for sacrificing, not for litigating. Nor ought those who are called thrones of God (Council of Toledo XI, c. 5) to be disturbed by the plots of depraved men, but [ought] freely to serve Christ the Lord.

XVIII. Although the bishops of a province, together with their metropolitan, may deal with the cases of bishops of their province in charity and concord, they may not, however (as was established in the aforesaid synod in your presence), decide them without the authority of the Roman pontiff. But if anything otherwise is presumed by some, those who have done this shall suffer the penalty of their presumption: and those who have been wrongly excommunicated or condemned by them shall be absolved and restored by the authority of this holy see and by the power of our blessed teacher Peter, the key-bearer. For the Lord himself says: Whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven (Matthew XVI).

XIX. Whenever bishops think they are being unduly burdened by their fellow bishops of the province (Hadrian 6 and 18, from canons 4 and 7 of the Council of Serdica) or by the metropolitan, or hold them under suspicion, let them at once appeal to the Roman see, to which they shall be allowed to go freely without any detention or seizure of their property. And while they have appealed to the aforesaid Roman mother Church, or have requested to be heard by her, let no one presume either to excommunicate them, or to take away their sees, or to remove their property, or to do them any violence, before their case is concluded by the authority of the Roman pontiff. But if anything otherwise is presumed by anyone, it shall be nothing, and shall lack force. For we do not presume this wrongly, but you know well, Athanasius, that this very thing was established at the synod of Nicaea, and that our predecessors acted [on it]: since when you and Paul of Constantinople, Asclepas of Gaza, and Lucius of Adrianople were condemned by the Eastern bishops without consulting Julius of holy memory, our predecessor, and fled to him as to the head of the whole world (as has always been permitted to this holy see), having learned of their wickedness (Tripartite [History] IV, 15, from Sozomen III, 7) and your righteousness, he received you into communion, and, taking care of you all on account of the dignity of his own see, and restoring to each his church, he wrote to the Easterners, blaming them for not having dealt rightly in expelling blameless men from their churches, and for not observing the decrees of the council of Nicaea. Of these he ordered some to appear before him on a fixed day, so that they might give a definite account of such presumptions, and that he might show in their presence that he had issued a just decree concerning them. He also threatened that the brethren would not henceforth suffer such things, and that unless they ceased from presumptions of this kind, they would be removed from their own ranks. For by such a privilege of this holy see you and your brethren recovered your own churches, with everything belonging to them. By these and very many other proofs it is evident that no bishop who has appealed to this holy see, or has taken it as his defender, ought to be condemned or despoiled of his property, until he receives the judgement on him of our apostolic authority (Martin I, session 2 of the Lateran Council), that is, of Peter, prince of the apostles, because Christ Jesus entrusted this to this holy see alone, that is, the apostolic [see], inasmuch as the aforesaid prince of the apostles alone and before all was entrusted with, and was found worthy to receive from Christ God, the King of kings, the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Matthew XVI).

XX. Concerning the delays for bishops (in the Decretum of Ivo, book IV), about which you consulted [us], we find that different rules were laid down by the fathers. For some ordered that a year or six months be granted, to repel the schemes of those attacking them, to prepare their own replies, to secure witnesses, and to seek the counsel of bishops and friends; but others [ordered] a year, on which most agree. Less, however (see Council of Carthage III, chapter 7), than six months I have not found, since these [delays] are granted even to laymen; how much more to the priests of the Lord! For it has also often been forbidden by our predecessors and by the other holy fathers that anyone should bring disparagements against the priests of the Lord; how much more accusations not brought forth from the root of charity! 'Be quiet,' they say, 'and do not persecute those who serve God perfectly, by whose prayers both earthly wars are calmed and the assaults of the angels who withdrew from God are driven off, and who by the constancy of their prayers confound all the demons who are corrupted' (Tripartite History VII, 9). For delays are to be granted not within a narrow time but over a long space, so that the accused may be able to prepare themselves, to meet all those in communion with them who are placed in the provinces, to prepare witnesses, and to arm themselves fully against those who plot against them.

XXI. For judges and accusers ought to be those who are free of all suspicion (Hadrian 15), and who wish to put forward their opinion from the root of charity. Therefore, these things having been set forth as much lawfully (Tripartite History IX, 14, from Theodoret V, 9) as canonically, we ask also that the reverence of all Christians rejoice together in them, with spiritual love and the fear of the Lord intervening, by which human offence is removed and the building up of the churches is put before everything, so that all may labour rather for the building up of the brethren than for their condemnation; since the Lord says: By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another (John XIII). For we have already given the pattern (Damasus, letter 2, from Tripartite History IX, 15; from Theodoret V, 10), and we know that it was given by our predecessors, that if anyone acknowledges himself a Christian, he should keep what is known to have been handed down by the apostles, as the apostle Paul says: If anyone announces to you anything other than what you have received, let him be anathema (Galatians I). For Christ the Son of God, our Lord, granted to the human race the fullest salvation by his own passion, to free us (Romans VIII). And if God loved us so much that he did not spare even his own Son, but handed him over for us all, to free us: why do we not love the brethren, or judge them rashly, when the aforesaid apostle says: Do not judge one another, but rather judge this, that you do not put a stumbling block or an offence before a brother (Romans XIV)? For if those who love the brethren are born of God and see God, what then will those be who persecute them, and strive to condemn them by disparaging, scheming, accusing and harassing? If those are sons of God, these without doubt are sons of the devil, who always, as a roaring lion goes about seeking whom he may devour (I Peter V), so pursue the brethren in order to destroy them. And those who shrink from helping the brethren acquire a greater burden of sins, and are found guilty [of withholding] the comfort of brotherhood. Woe, says the prophet, to him who gives his friend drink, mixing in his gall (Habakkuk II). And again the most wise Solomon says: For he who speaks wicked things cannot be hidden, nor will the judgement that rebukes pass him by. For in the thoughts of the ungodly there will be an inquiry; and the hearing of his words will reach God, for the rebuke of his iniquities: for the ear of jealousy hears all things, and the tumult of those who murmur will not be hidden (Wisdom I). For if they had been willing to embrace these things with their own sound sense, they would by no means slip into reprobation, but, through the fear of God taking care to guard their words, they would surely preserve the pious definition of the holy fathers without any presumption of harm: since sacred scripture says: Good counsel will preserve you, and a good mind will guard you (Proverbs II). For such accusations and disparagements do not proceed spiritually from the saving springs (Maurus of Cesena, letter in the same council) toward the gaining of eternal life, and therefore blessed Paul fittingly admonishes us, saying: Not to be wiser than one ought to be wise, but to be wise unto sobriety (Romans XII). Let us persevere in the definition of piety. For those who pass it by are not only themselves falling from their own firmness, but have left to all a memorial of their foolishness, so that in the things in which they sinned they could by no means remain hidden. For glory and disgrace are in speech, and in a man's tongue is his fall (Ecclesiasticus V). And therefore it is fitting that this exposure of their faults be inserted into our acts, so that you may no longer suffer such things while they sow tares and offences, but may be found worthy to rejoice in your offices and doctrines. Let them therefore blush at such things, and hasten to withdraw blasphemy of this kind, if they do not wish to be separated from our priestly college and torn away from the fellowship of the Christian people. For although we could have said and written many and very necessary things about these matters, which are found established in the decrees of the apostolic see and by the apostles and their successors, namely our predecessors, it nevertheless seemed better to us to close the letter with a prayer (Julius to the church of Alexandria, Tripartite History IV, 29). May God almighty, and his only-begotten Son and our Saviour Jesus Christ, grant you this incentive: that you help with all your strength all our brethren and fellow bishops who labour under any tribulations whatever, and, suffering with them, carry the cross of the same Lord and Saviour, so that you may appear before all as his true disciples, so that both you and those who are with you may possess, here and in the future, the better things which eye has not seen, nor have they entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him (I Corinthians II), through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father almighty for ages of ages, amen. I wish you farewell, dearest brethren. Given on the Ides of February, in the consulship of Agarius and Julian, most illustrious men.
SECOND LETTER OF POPE FELIX II
TO THE SAME AND TO THE OTHER PRIESTS OF THE LORD.
On the patient endurance of persecutions and tribulations.

Felix, pope of the holy universal Church, and by the grace of God bishop of the catholic and apostolic Church of the city of Rome, together with our holy council of most reverend priests who have assembled here with us (Pope Martin I, in the synodal letter of the Lateran Council), for the confirmation of the most pious doctrines of the catholic Church and the relief of oppressed brethren, namely our fellow bishops who hold the right faith of the Council of Nicaea and who do not harass the brethren, to all our spiritual brethren and the others consecrated to the Lord in the priestly college, and to the whole fullness of the catholic Church.

Grace and peace be multiplied to you in the strengthening and communion of the Holy Spirit, so that, advancing in him from glory to glory, we may proclaim the virtues of him who called us out of darkness into his marvellous light (I Peter II), with whom there is no change nor shadow of alteration. We exhort you, brethren (James I), to bear persecutions and tribulations patiently, so that you may be found sons of him whom daily you call Father, God in heaven; and that you may overcome all things in him who overcame all things for our sake: who also did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all (Romans VIII). It is fitting too that imitators of God imitate God in every word and deed (Maximus of Aquileia, session 4 of the same Lateran Council held in the year 649). And therefore we ought to say what the Lord himself declared of himself: The prince of this world will come, and will find nothing in me (John XIV). Those too have come who persecute you and us, for they cannot persecute you without us, since we are members of the one God, and through his sanctification we hold his one priesthood, and they have found nothing of their own in us: for whatever we are, we are by the grace of God, although for that reason they have striven irrationally to slander us, as enemies are wont to do, hastening thereby to cover up their own madness, so that by falsehood they may be able to overshadow the truth. For I have written to you, says the blessed apostle, with many tears, not that you should be saddened, but that you may know what charity I have more abundantly towards you (II Corinthians II). For to disparage those who disparage (Deusdedit, bishop of Cagliari, in the same place) is not good, lest, roused by the things that have been written, we make a contest of injury. We ought not at all to fear the reproach of men (Martin I, session 3 in the same place), nor to be overcome by their reproaches, since the Lord commands us this through the prophet Isaiah, saying: Hear me, you who know judgement, my people, in whose hearts is my law (Isaiah LI). Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies (Psalm XLIII). Considering also what is written in the psalm: Will not God search out these things? For he knows the secrets of the heart, and the thoughts of such men, that they are vain. And each one has spoken vain things to his neighbour, deceitful lips, with a double heart they have spoken evil things. But the Lord will destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue. They have said: Our lips are our own; who is our lord (Psalm XI)? For if they kept these things in memory, they would by no means leap forth into such great iniquity. For (the words of the same pope) they do this not through approved and fatherly teaching, but in order to exercise their vengeance on the servants of God. For it is written: The way of the fool is right in his own eyes. And there are ways which seem just to a man, but their end leads to death (Proverbs XII, XIV). For we who suffer these things ought to reserve them to the judgement of God (Third Roman Council, under Symmachus), who will render to each according to his works (Jeremiah XV). He also thundered through his ministers, saying: Vengeance is mine, I will repay (Romans XII). Do you, then, in right faith and with pure and good will help one another in turn, and let no one withdraw his hand from supporting a brother: since by this, says the Lord, all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another (John XIII). Hence he himself also speaks through the prophet, saying: Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell in unity (Psalm CXXXII). I mean in a spiritual dwelling (Paul, bishop of Constantinople, a Monothelite, to Pope Theodore, session 4 of the Lateran Council) and in the concord which is in God, and in the unity of this delightful faith, according to the truth of the dwelling, which was especially adorned in Aaron and in those who put on priestly dignity, like ointment upon the head, watering the principal understanding and leading it down to the very furthest knowledge. For in this dwelling the Lord promised blessing and eternal life. Embracing, therefore, the merit of this prophetic utterance, we have set out the present brotherly letter, seeking, and intending to seek, by no means our own things, for charity's sake. For it is not good to disparage those who disparage, or, according to the common saying, to knock out a stake with a stake. Far be it. These things are not ours: wherefore may the Godhead turn them away. Our habits have not been taught to conquer in this way, but in the patience of long-suffering and in the spirit of humility: for just as fennel-flower (to speak prophetically) is by no means cleaned by hardness (Daniel III), so neither is the restful fruit of peace and understanding pressed out by harshness. For this reason we have also borne the blows of words, so that we may be able at least little by little to imitate him who deigned to humble himself for our sake, and through this stroke may avoid the words of that final vengeance. Let us hear, therefore, and agree with the orator of the Church, who through the tongue of the Holy Spirit cries out with a clear voice, saying: Let all things among you be done in charity (I Corinthians XVI). So whether we inquire, or only speak, and are only heard, let charity intervene. Let some art exist for the composing and joining of good concord. For it is fitting that we, inquiring about God and counting up the intentions of our mind with a spirit of uprightness, should peacefully dwell in the temple for him, for the sake of the Lord, who spoke through the prophet: If you seek, seek, and dwell with me (Isaiah XXI, according to the Septuagint). For God has given us as a mirror to his people, and those who have been appointed by God to obtain the priesthood ought so to move towards one another in humility of the mind's steps, that those who look to us may be built up for the better, rather than (it grieves me to say it) that the path of their feet be shaken by our discord. Let us incline ourselves to concord, and be of one mind in charity. Let us revere humility, through which the height of the spirit is wont to be grasped. For if until now we have loved silence more than garrulity of words, we have thought this indeed to be well, lest by answering your writings in kind we should stir up the tinder of injury, and be judged faint-hearted by him who proclaimed that all things should be directed towards charity. And we prayed then that a door of guard be set upon our lips, and to conceive an unsounded word rather than a sounding word: and yet this is a gift to me from the Lord, and I became as a man who does not hear, and who has no rebukes in his mouth (Psalm XVII). But since there is a time to speak and a time to be silent (Ecclesiastes III), I open the word, and close the door of silence, fittingly praying: Lord, you will open my lips, and I shall answer a word to those who reproach me (Psalm L, CXVIII). For although we have been silent, we shall not always be silent, as the Lord opens to us the keys of the word. Accordingly the *apocrisiarii* [envoys] sent at present by your brotherly beatitude, after many discordant discussions held among us concerning the ecclesiastical inquiry, came in the end to this: admonishing and urging us to interpret the understanding of the will of the one true Christ our God, and to send an interpretation of this kind to your most sacred reverence. We, however, accepting the admonition of the good conscience of the aforesaid venerable men, and knowing also what the summit of the principate of the apostles teaches (I Peter III), to be ready to give satisfaction to everyone who asks a word concerning the hope which is in us, according to the fear of God, tempering gentleness with good knowledge, set out our mind through this letter on this inquiry alone, avoiding and guarding against superfluous exercise and wrangling of words, because of surfeit and the unsuitability of the present time, understanding, putting forward or saying nothing at all other than what we have heard and learned from the holy and universal great apostles and their successors, and [what] our fathers have recounted to us, and, having heard, we have preached, pressing towards the heavenly calling. Ours is the endeavour where the establishment of peace remains for those who are in the arena of piety; well is the one glory and crown given to the intercessor. We have been made manifest to God, who judges and tests all things. We do not stand contentiously, we do not look to contradiction, nor do we embrace empty favour: but we are known to have made the resolution of this inquiry by setting forth the word of God, trusting that the Lord God of peace will preserve unity and love towards one another among us in the glory of his most kindly majesty. We, and those who are with us, greet warmly all the brotherhood that is with your beatitude in Christ. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of Philemon and Atticus, most illustrious men.
